# Two Restructurings Is Already the Diagnosis (continued)

*Picking up at the fork, where the previous note ran out.*

A short recap of the position, because everything below depends on it. Cost has been removed twice without touching the loss, which locates the loss somewhere other than the cost base. The order book is shrinking in a way that looks less like market weather and more like the exhaust of the two restructurings. The managers are pricing the asset with their feet, and they're better informed than anyone who will sit in the room. The board has asked for a credible path, not for profitability — a distinction worth securing in writing before month eleven, when it will be too late to secure anything.

What follows is the part that actually decides it: where profit could live, what the year looks like, and what we do if it can't live anywhere.

---

## Where the profit is, if it's anywhere

I'd resist naming the answer before the contract-level cash P&L lands. But it would be coy to pretend the shape is unknown. In industrial services the profit pools are remarkably consistent, and they share one property: something stops the customer from running a tender.

**Work that is mandated rather than chosen.** Statutory inspection, regulated maintenance, environmental monitoring, licensed handling. The customer isn't buying a service, they're buying an absence of liability. Price holds. Renewal is near-automatic. Nobody optimises the third decimal place on a compliance line item.

**Work tied to an installed base we uniquely understand.** Aftermarket on equipment the group's profitable divisions built and sold — proprietary parts, technical data, warranty interaction, the engineer who knows why that unit trips in August. This is the one line with genuine asymmetry, and I'd want to know immediately how much of it we hold versus how much has leaked to third parties while we were restructuring. My expectation is that the leak is large and nobody has measured it, because measuring it implies a conversation between two divisions that don't especially enjoy each other.

**Emergency and shutdown work.** Unplannable, therefore unbiddable, therefore priceable. Margins in the high teens where the capability is real. It requires standing capacity, which is precisely what two rounds of cost reduction will have eaten first, since idle capacity is the easiest thing on a spreadsheet to mistake for waste.

**Dense clusters.** Wherever we have enough sites inside a travel radius that a van doesn't spend its day being a van. Density isn't a service line, but it's the multiplier on all of them, and it's the variable most often absent from the discussion.

And where the losses will be, with equal predictability: competitively tendered labour supply, where we are an expensive intermediary in a market that rewards nothing; lump-sum project and installation work, which imports completion risk onto a services balance sheet and is where surprises come from; the large national accounts that oblige us to hold a map we can't afford; and anything won in the last three years on price against a pure-play with a third of our overhead.

The interesting question isn't which of these is profitable. It's how much revenue we would have to be willing to lose. I'd expect the honest answer to be somewhere between half and two-thirds — and I'd expect the organisation's capacity to accept that number to be the binding constraint on the whole exercise, not analysis, not capital, not the market.

Worth asking aloud, once, early: is anyone in this building actually prepared to run a business a third of the current size? Because if not, we've chosen exit already and are simply taking a year to say so.

---

## The year

Days 1–90 are in the earlier note: retention locks, a bid freeze below a hurdle rate, contract-level cash P&L, the liability tail opened, both workstreams live and neither labelled the fallback. From there:

**Month 4 — the scope decision.** A named list of contracts, service lines, and geographies we will no longer serve, with exit mechanics attached: notice periods, novation candidates, break costs, the sequence that avoids all the pain landing in one quarter. Cost then leaves as a consequence. This is the day the exercise either becomes real or becomes the third restructuring with a better name; I'd want the list signed by someone whose next job doesn't depend on the revenue on it.

**Months 4–6 — the repricing wave, run as an experiment rather than a campaign.** Price rises into the retained book, staged so we learn from the early ones. What matters isn't the yield, it's the *loss rate* — which customers walk, at what increase, in which lines. That distribution is the asymmetry test, and it's the closest thing to a structural verdict we will ever hold in our hands.

**Month 6 — the fork.** Not a decision. A checkpoint with three possible readings, and I'd write the readings down in month one so we can't invent them later:

- *Execution-driven.* Pure-plays earn a real return on the same work in the same places; price holds where we push it; the retained core makes positive contribution before allocation. Recovery gets the second half.
- *Structural.* Nobody makes money in these lines, price won't move anywhere, density is unrecoverable at any credible size. Separation gets the second half and we stop spending management attention on a plan whose conclusion is already visible.
- *Mixed*, which is what it will be. Part of the book is a real business and part of it never was. This is the reading people find hardest, because it produces neither a turnaround story nor a clean exit, and it is almost certainly the true one.

**Months 7–12, recovery branch.** Not a profit target — a run-rate and a set of proof points a sceptical outsider could verify: margin-weighted backlog rising while revenue falls; win rate holding at higher prices; the critical thirty still here; the benchmark gap closing by a stated fraction; one clean month of positive contribution after honestly-caused overhead. Twelve months cannot produce a profitable year in a business with multi-year contracts. It can produce evidence that only has one interpretation.

**Months 7–12, separation branch.** Vendor due diligence complete, perimeter drawn, tail quantified and either allocated or reserved, buyer conversations already warm because the data room was built in month two rather than in a panic in month ten.

The two branches share their first six months almost entirely. That convergence is the most valuable feature of the situation and I would defend it against every request for early clarity, however sincerely those requests are made on morale grounds. Ambiguity held deliberately is not indecision; it's the only thing standing between us and a distressed price.

---

## Exit, which is more than one thing

The framing "turnaround or divestment" contains an assumption I'd gently decline: that the unit is a single object with a single fate.

**Trade sale to a pure-play consolidator.** The natural buyer. They already carry the overhead, they want the density, and they'll pay for route economics we can't monetise. Best price for the clusters, and only available with a clean perimeter and the people still in place.

**Sponsor platform.** Buys a management team and a fragmented market. Requires the managers we are currently losing. Every week of delay on retention narrows this door.

**Management buyout.** Consider the inversion here. The people leaving may not be pessimistic about the business; they may be pessimistic about the business *inside this group* — the allocation, the internal discount vehicle, the two restructurings, the approval layers. Those constraints don't travel with a sale. Their exit is a signal about ownership as much as economics, and the cheapest way to test which is to ask a small number of them a hypothetical question and listen to how fast the answer arrives.

**Break-up, which I suspect is the real answer.** Repatriate the installed-base aftermarket into the equipment divisions where the asymmetry actually sits and where the margin will finally be visible to whoever owns it. Sell the dense clusters to the consolidator. Run off or novate the tail. Higher aggregate value than a whole-unit sale, more work, more stranded cost, and it dissolves the unit as an organisational entity rather than transferring it — which is why it will be the least popular option in the room and worth putting on the table first, quietly, before positions harden.

**Partial sale with a supply agreement.** Sell the majority, retain a minority stake and a long-term service arrangement covering the shared customers. This is the answer to the pull-through hostage argument if the repricing test shows the pull-through is real. It keeps the bundle and removes the P&L, and it's rarely considered because it isn't a clean story.

**White-label partnership — no transaction at all.** A pure-play delivers under our name to the shared accounts; we keep the relationship, they keep the vans. Cheaper and faster than a sale, reversible, and it can be piloted in one region in month five as a live test of whether the customers care who holds the wrench. My guess is that they don't, and that finding out costs almost nothing.

**Orderly run-off.** No buyer for a business, but there are always buyers for contracts and depots. This is the floor, and its value must be calculated early — not as a plan, but because it's the reserve price, and negotiating without one is how good assets go cheap.

---

## Choosing

I'd fix the thresholds in month one, before we know any of the answers, because criteria written after the evidence arrives are not criteria. They're commentary.

*Exit unless all of the following hold:*

The retained core, reconstructed after the scope decision, makes positive contribution before allocation and covers the overhead it genuinely causes — with a path to a return above the group's cost of capital inside thirty-six months, at a size someone is willing to actually run.

Independent operators earn a real margin on the same work in the same geographies. If nobody does, managerial talent is not the missing input and we should stop shopping for it.

Price moved somewhere. A book with no line on which we can raise price has no defence, and its losses are structural by definition.

The critical thirty are still here. Both branches need them; recovery needs them more, and dies first without them.

The pull-through survived repricing — the divisions chose to pay rather than to let the concession go. If they declined, the strategic argument was already dead and we simply hadn't asked the question in a form that produced an answer.

And the comparison that decides it: risk-weighted value of the retained business, minus the capital and management attention the recovery consumes, against net proceeds now plus stranded cost plus whatever tail refuses to leave. Attention belongs in that sum. It's the group's scarcest input and it's the one nobody prices.

If the tests split — and they will — the answer is the third option rather than a compromise between the first two. Keep what has asymmetry, and put it where the asymmetry lives. Sell what has density to someone whose economics reward density. Close the rest without ceremony.

One last thing, offered rather than argued. The most likely reason this ends badly is not that we misdiagnose it. It's that a plan arrives in month ten that is recognisably the second restructuring with new adjectives, and it will be plausible, and it will be produced by people acting in good faith who cannot see the shape they're inside. The defence against that isn't vigilance. It's having built the separation option properly, in parallel, from week one — so that when the moment comes, the alternative already exists and doesn't need to be won in a meeting.

That's the whole design, really. Not to make the right decision. To arrive at the decision with both options genuinely open, and let the evidence do what argument won't.
